passage:
Saturday
Today Francis and I went to see the dinosaur movie at the mall. Papa paid for the tickets and popcorn. After twenty minutes I was so bored. The dinosaurs only talked and talked. Francis whispered, "Let's go and play in the arcade." But I said no, because Papa had paid a lot of money, and if we left, the money would be wasted. So we sat for one and a half more hours. I nearly fell asleep. When we came out it was too late for the arcade. Papa asked if it was good. I said yes because he paid. He ruffled my hair and said, "That's my boy." My back hurts from sitting.
Samir

qa.q: What did Francis suggest after twenty minutes?
qa.a: Francis whispered, "Let's go and play in the arcade."

qa.q: Why did Samir stay for the whole movie even though he was bored?
qa.a: Papa had paid a lot, so leaving felt like wasting the money; Samir didn't see that the money was spent either way and only the time could still be saved.

qa.q: What could Samir think about the next time a paid-for thing turns boring?
qa.a: He could ask whether staying will make the next hour any better, since the money is already gone, and tell Papa honestly that it was boring.

qa.q: How might Francis feel about sitting through the movie?
qa.a: Francis probably felt bored and a bit disappointed about missing the arcade, after suggesting it so early.

grounding: Shows a boy sitting through a boring paid-for movie because leaving would feel like wasting the money.

passage: At the temple fair in their village near Madurai, Ramesh spent his whole ten rupees on a big, bright green sweet from a cart. One bite, and his face twisted. It tasted like soap and far too much sugar. His sister Aparna laughed. "Give it to the crows." "No! It cost ten rupees!" Ramesh took another bite, then another, chewing slowly with his eyes shut. His Ammamma, Rukmini, watched from the bangle stall. "Kanna, are you enjoying it?" she asked. "No," he said, taking another bite. "But I paid." By the time he finished, his stomach felt heavy, and he had no appetite for the hot bajji his Ammamma bought for everyone.

qa.q: How much did the green sweet cost?
qa.a: The sweet cost ten rupees.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh keep eating a sweet he disliked?
qa.a: Spending ten rupees made giving it away feel like losing the money, so he kept eating even though it tasted bad and made him feel heavy.

qa.q: What could Ammamma say to help Ramesh with this kind of choice?
qa.a: She could gently point out that the ten rupees are gone either way and eating more only adds a bad feeling, so next time he can stop and save room for something he likes.

qa.q: How might Aparna see her brother's choice?
qa.a: Aparna finds it funny and a little silly, since to her the obvious answer was to give the sweet to the crows.

grounding: Shows a boy eating a sweet he dislikes because he paid for it, even though finishing it spoils the rest of his evening.

passage: It was raining in Madrid, and Marek had been playing the same slow puzzle game on the family tablet for an hour. He had stopped enjoying it after ten minutes. The levels were all the same: push a box, push another box. His friend Santiago, who lived downstairs, knocked on the door holding a football. "Rain's stopped! Park?" Marek didn't look up. "I can't stop now. I've already played an hour. If I quit, it's all for nothing." Santiago waited, bouncing the ball, then shrugged and went down alone. Marek pushed another box. Then another. When he finally put the tablet down, it was dark and raining again.

qa.q: What was Santiago holding when he knocked on the door?
qa.a: Santiago was holding a football.

qa.q: Why did Marek feel he couldn't stop playing?
qa.a: Marek felt stuck, because he had already put in an hour and quitting felt like throwing that hour away. He kept going even though he was bored and the next hour would be just the same.

qa.q: What question could help Marek decide next time?
qa.a: He could ask, "If I were starting now, would I choose this game or the park?" The hour already spent can't come back either way.

qa.q: How might Santiago feel going down to the park alone?
qa.a: Santiago may feel disappointed and a bit confused, since the rain had stopped and Marek didn't even seem to be having fun.

grounding: Shows a boy continuing a boring game because he has already spent an hour on it, missing the chance to play outside.

passage: At the school canteen, Wasim, nine, bought a spicy paneer roll with his own twenty rupees. One bite and his eyes watered. He hated it. "Are you going to finish that?" asked Devika from his class, eating her plain idli. "I paid twenty rupees," Wasim said, and took another bite. His face turned red. He drank half his water bottle. He took another bite. "You don't even like it," Devika said. "But I paid." He chewed slowly, miserable, while the others ran out to play. By the last bite recess was almost over. Devika waited at the door. "You missed kho-kho," she said. Wasim wiped his eyes. "I didn't want to waste the money." "The money was already gone," Devika said. "You just wasted recess too."

qa.q: How much did Wasim pay for the paneer roll?
qa.a: Twenty rupees.

qa.q: Why did Wasim keep eating a roll he hated?
qa.a: He felt it would be a waste to stop because he had already paid, so he kept eating, miserable, even though the money was gone either way.

qa.q: What could Wasim do next time he buys something he doesn't like?
qa.a: He could stop after the first bites and ask himself what he wants to do now, like go and play, since eating more won't bring the twenty rupees back.

qa.q: How might Devika feel waiting at the door for Wasim?
qa.a: She probably felt a bit impatient and sorry for him, since he missed kho-kho for a roll he didn't even enjoy.

grounding: A boy keeps eating a spicy roll he hates because he paid for it, and misses recess games.

passage: I'm Leela. Last Sunday, visiting my friend Seema, I watched her son Tinku, ten, play a long property-trading board game with his cousins. The game had gone on for an hour and a half. The cousins had drifted off to the terrace. Tinku stayed, rolling for everyone, yawning. "Tinku, come play cricket," Seema called. "No, Mummy! I've been playing for ages. If I stop now, all that time is wasted." I can't say what he was thinking, but he kept going another half hour, sighing at every turn. By the time he packed it away, the cricket had ended. He sat on the steps, cross. Seema sat next to him and said softly, "The time was spent anyway, beta. The only question was what to do next."

qa.q: How long had the game gone on when the cousins gave up?
qa.a: The game had gone on for an hour and a half.

qa.q: Why might Tinku have kept playing a game he found boring?
qa.a: He seemed to feel that stopping would waste all the time already spent, so he kept going, bored and sighing, as if carrying on protected it.

qa.q: When Seema called him to cricket, what choice would have served Tinku better?
qa.a: He could have asked himself what he wanted to do now and gone to play cricket, since more board-game time wouldn't give back the hour and a half.

qa.q: How might Seema have felt watching Tinku sit alone with the game?
qa.a: Seema probably felt a mix of amusement and sympathy, and chose a gentle word afterward instead of a lecture.

grounding: A family friend watches a boy keep playing a boring board game alone because he has already spent so long on it.

passage: Last Sunday at the fair, I bought a big cone of candy floss with my own pocket money. After four bites it was too sweet and my teeth felt funny. But it had cost thirty rupees, so I kept eating. My sister Sonali said, "Joseph, just throw it. You don't even like it." I said, "No! I paid for it!" I ate it all, slowly, while we walked, and then my tummy hurt on the ride. I didn't even enjoy the giant wheel. Later I thought: the thirty rupees were gone anyway, whether I ate it or not. Eating it didn't bring them back. It only made the giant wheel worse. Next time I think I'll stop when it stops being nice.

qa.q: How much did the candy floss cost?
qa.a: Thirty rupees.

qa.q: Why did Joseph keep eating after it stopped tasting nice?
qa.a: Joseph felt guilty about wasting something already paid for, so eating it felt right even while it spoiled the day.

qa.q: What does Joseph plan to do next time, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Stop when it stops being nice, because the money is gone either way and eating more only spoils the rest of the fair.

qa.q: How does Sonali see Joseph's choice?
qa.a: Sonali sees that Joseph doesn't like it and thinks throwing it away is sensible.

grounding: A child recalls finishing candy floss that had stopped tasting nice because it was paid for, and later seeing the money was gone either way.

passage:
Camp counsellor's note, Day 3, summer camp, Nashik
During free time Kiran started the thousand-piece jigsaw of a ship. After twenty minutes he was yawning and said it was "the most boring puzzle in the world." When Jagdish invited him to the cricket match outside, he refused: "I've already done a whole hour on this. If I stop now it's a waste." He stayed at the table another forty minutes, sighing, placing hardly any pieces, while the others played. At snack time he looked unhappy and said he "didn't get to do anything fun today." I sat with him and asked, "If you walked in now and saw this puzzle, would you start it?" He said no, straight away. Tomorrow I will remind him he can choose again.

qa.q: What did Kiran say when Jagdish invited him to play cricket?
qa.a: "I've already done a whole hour on this. If I stop now it's a waste."

qa.q: Why did Kiran stay at the puzzle even though he was bored?
qa.a: He felt it would be a waste to give up after an hour, so stopping felt worse than staying, even though he was unhappy.

qa.q: Why is the counsellor's question a helpful one?
qa.a: Asking whether he would start the puzzle now makes Kiran judge the choice from this moment, not from the hour already spent.

qa.q: How might Jagdish feel when Kiran refuses to join the match?
qa.a: Jagdish may feel a little disappointed, since he wanted Kiran to play with them.

grounding: A camp counsellor records a boy who keeps doing a puzzle he finds boring because he has already spent an hour on it.

passage:
Saturday
I am on page 212 of the dragon book and I still don't like it. The dragons don't even fly until page 180, and then they just talk. Madhav finished a funny detective book in two days and started another one. He said, "Santosh, why are you still reading that?" I said, "Because I've read 212 pages! If I stop, all that reading was for nothing." Then I read three more pages and fell asleep. Amma found me snoring on the book. She said, "Kanna, those pages are read already. They stay read. You can pick a book you'll actually enjoy." I am thinking about it. But 212 pages is a LOT.
Santosh

qa.q: How many pages of the dragon book has Santosh read?
qa.a: 212 pages.

qa.q: Why does Santosh keep reading a book that isn't fun?
qa.a: Santosh feels that stopping would make all that reading a waste, and that thought feels worse than being bored.

qa.q: What does Amma point out that could help Santosh choose?
qa.a: That the pages already read stay read, so the choice can be about which book would be enjoyable from now on.

qa.q: How does Madhav see Santosh's reading?
qa.a: Madhav is puzzled why Santosh keeps going with a book that isn't fun, since he simply starts a new one.

grounding: A child's diary shows forcing through a disliked book because of the pages already read.

passage: At the Dussehra fair in their village near Nashik, Siddharth, nine, bought a big plate of jalebis with his pocket money. After two bites he didn't like them. Too sticky, too sweet. But he kept eating. "I paid ten rupees," he told his cousin Yash. "I have to finish." His stomach started to hurt. Yash offered to throw the rest away. "No! Then my money is wasted." Siddharth ate another one, slowly, frowning. Then another. By the last one, he felt sick. He sat on the steps of the temple while the other children ran to the giant wheel. He had no money left for the ride, and his stomach ached. "At least I didn't waste the jalebis," he said weakly.

qa.q: How much did Siddharth pay for the jalebis?
qa.a: Ten rupees.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth keep eating jalebis he didn't like?
qa.a: He felt reluctant to waste the ten rupees, so the money already spent felt like a reason to continue, even though he was miserable and sick.

qa.q: What could Siddharth do next time he doesn't like something he paid for?
qa.a: He could stop when he dislikes it, since the money is already spent either way, and save his stomach for something he enjoys.

qa.q: How might Yash see Siddharth's choice?
qa.a: Yash probably thinks it's silly and a bit worrying, since he offered to throw the rest away.

grounding: It shows a child who keeps eating food he dislikes because it was paid for, treating past spending as a reason to continue.

passage: In Lima, on a rainy Saturday, Mateo and his friend Chidi started a long board game about building railways. After twenty minutes, Mateo was bored. He didn't like the rules. After forty minutes, he was more bored. Chidi yawned and said, "Want to play football in the hall instead?" Mateo shook his head. "We've already played for forty minutes. If we stop now, it's all wasted." So they kept going. An hour passed. Then an hour and a half. Mateo yawned and kept rolling the dice. By the time they finished, the rain had stopped and it was too dark to go outside. Mateo put the pieces in the box, feeling tired and grumpy. "At least we finished," he said. Chidi didn't answer.

qa.q: How long had they played when Chidi suggested football?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Mateo refuse to stop the boring game?
qa.a: He felt the forty minutes already spent would be wasted, so past effort felt like a reason to continue even though he was bored and grumpy.

qa.q: What could Mateo ask himself next time he's bored with a game?
qa.a: He could ask whether he wants to keep playing from now on, since the time already spent is gone either way.

qa.q: What is it like for Chidi to keep playing?
qa.a: Chidi seems bored and frustrated, having offered a better option and been refused.

grounding: It shows a child who keeps playing a boring game because he has already spent time on it, treating past effort as a reason to continue.

passage: In the school canteen, Shankar bought a new dish he'd never tried: bitter-gourd curry with rice. It was twenty rupees, his whole lunch money. One bite and he made a face. Too bitter. His friend Deepika said, "Leave it, share my parathas." Shankar shook his head. "I paid twenty rupees. I have to eat it." He forced down spoon after spoon. His eyes watered. Deepika's parathas smelled lovely next to him. By the end, his tongue felt strange and he had missed the chance to play at break. "I finished it," he said proudly, but his face was pale. Deepika shrugged. "The money was gone anyway, Shankar. You could have had parathas."

qa.q: How much did the bitter-gourd curry cost?
qa.a: Twenty rupees.

qa.q: Why did Shankar feel he had to finish the curry?
qa.a: He felt stubborn and worried about wasting the twenty rupees, so the money already spent felt like a reason to keep eating despite the taste.

qa.q: What does Deepika point out that could help Shankar?
qa.a: The money was gone anyway, so he could have enjoyed her parathas instead of forcing down food he didn't like.

qa.q: How does Deepika seem to feel watching Shankar eat?
qa.a: Deepika seems puzzled and a bit sorry for him, offering parathas and gently pointing out the choice.

grounding: It shows a child who keeps eating a dish he dislikes because he paid for it, treating past spending as a reason to continue.

passage:
Monday, winter holidays. Jatin opened a new 1000-piece jigsaw of a boring grey bridge. He found it dull after ten minutes. But he'd spent his whole birthday money on it.

Wednesday. Jatin had done the edges. His back hurt. Imran came to call him for cricket. "Two more hours," Jatin said. "I've already done so much."

Saturday. Jatin was still hunched over the grey bridge. Imran came again. "Are you even having fun?"

"No. But if I stop now, all those hours are wasted."

"They're gone anyway," Imran said. "Are the next hours going to be fun?"

Jatin looked at the grey pieces, then out of the window at the sunny street. He slowly put the lid on the box and went to get his bat.

qa.q: What was the jigsaw a picture of?
qa.a: A boring grey bridge.

qa.q: Why did Jatin keep doing the jigsaw even though it was dull?
qa.a: Jatin felt that stopping would waste the birthday money and hours already spent, so continuing felt necessary even though he was bored.

qa.q: What question from Imran helped Jatin decide, and why?
qa.a: Imran asked whether the next hours would be fun, which turned Jatin's thinking toward what comes next rather than what was already spent.

qa.q: How might Imran have felt when Jatin kept saying no to cricket?
qa.a: Imran probably felt disappointed and a bit puzzled, missing his friend during the holidays.

grounding: Over several holiday days, a child keeps doing a dull jigsaw because he already spent money and hours on it.

passage:
Tanvir, you won't leave that boring film because you've paid for the ticket? Let your Pradeep dadu tell you about the Durga Puja fair when I was nine.

I had saved all my coins for a big plate of fried fish. One bite, and I hated it.

But I'd paid! So I sat on the bench and ate the whole plate. My friends were on the giant wheel, laughing.

That night I had a stomach ache and had missed the giant wheel.

My grandmother said something I've never forgotten. "The coins were gone the moment you paid. The only thing you could still save was your evening."

So, Tanvir, the ticket money is already spent. What's the best way to spend the next hour?

qa.q: What did young Pradeep buy with the coins?
qa.a: A big plate of fried fish.

qa.q: Why did young Pradeep eat the whole plate even though he hated it?
qa.a: Young Pradeep felt he had to because he had paid, and wasting the coins felt worse than being unhappy.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Pradeep's story, and what does it teach?
qa.a: His grandmother's words showed that the coins were gone either way, and the only thing he could still save was the evening.

qa.q: How might Pradeep's friends have felt on the giant wheel?
qa.a: The friends were happy and laughing, perhaps wondering why Pradeep wasn't joining them.

grounding: An elder recalls eating disliked food as a boy at a festival because it was paid for, and missing the fun.

passage:
It was Onam, the tour bus back to Kochi was leaving in twenty minutes, and Deepak was still at the table in the restaurant, staring at a huge plate of payasam he didn't like.

"Come on, Deepak," said his sister Vasudha. "The bus!"

"Papa paid for it. I have to finish."

He took another spoonful. Too sweet. His stomach already felt heavy. He took another.

"You don't even like it."

"But it's paid for. If I leave it, the money is wasted."

Vasudha sat down. "The money's already spent. Eating it won't bring it back. It'll just make you feel sick and miss the bus."

Deepak looked at the half-full plate. Then at the clock. He put the spoon down.

"Tell Papa thank you," he said, "but I'm full."

qa.q: How many minutes did Deepak have before the tour bus left?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Deepak keep eating payasam he didn't like?
qa.a: Deepak felt that leaving it would waste Papa's money, so finishing felt like the right thing even though his stomach felt heavy.

qa.q: What did Vasudha say that helped Deepak stop?
qa.a: Vasudha explained the money was already spent and eating it would only make him sick and miss the bus.

qa.q: How might Papa feel if he knew Deepak was forcing himself to eat?
qa.a: Papa would probably feel sorry and tell Deepak he never needed to finish food he didn't like.

grounding: Under time pressure during a festival, a child keeps eating food he dislikes because it was paid for.

passage: The colony's Diwali fair smelled of smoke and sugar. Madhav had begged for the tall paper cone of spicy chana, and Jagdish uncle at the stall had charged thirty rupees for it. Three bites in, his tongue burned and his eyes watered. He hated it. Still, he kept eating, one slow chickpea at a time, while sparklers fizzed near the gate. "Throw it, beta, you're crying," said his mother. "No! It cost thirty rupees," Madhav said, fanning his mouth. "If I throw it, the money is gone." He finished the whole cone on the steps with a red face and a steel tumbler of water, and missed the rangoli prize being announced.

qa.q: How much did the spicy chana cost?
qa.a: It cost thirty rupees.

qa.q: Why does Madhav keep eating the chana even though his tongue burns?
qa.a: He feels worried and a bit guilty that throwing it away would waste the thirty rupees, so finishing it feels like the careful, sensible thing to do.

qa.q: What could Madhav's mother say to help him next time?
qa.a: She could gently explain that the thirty rupees are spent whether he eats it or not, so he can stop and still enjoy the fair.

qa.q: How might Madhav's mother feel watching him finish the cone?
qa.a: She is probably worried and a little exasperated, seeing him suffer and miss the rangoli prize over money that was already spent.

grounding: Shows a child who keeps eating food he dislikes because it was paid for, treating past spending as a reason to continue.
